items.title: El Niño returns roughly every 2-7 years
items.claim: What is the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)?

options.text: A single tropical storm in the Pacific
A coupled ocean-atmosphere oscillation in the tropical Pacific recurring every 2-7 years; El Niño (warm central/eastern Pacific) and La Niña (cool) reshape global rainfall, drought and storm patterns
An annual cycle in the Arctic

items.reveal:
El Niño: weakened or reversed trade winds, warming of central and eastern equatorial Pacific, shifted convection. Typical effects: drought in Australia, Indonesia, parts of southern Africa; floods in coastal Peru and Ecuador; weaker Atlantic hurricane season; warmer global average.

La Niña: the opposite. The 1997-98 El Niño was among the strongest; 2015-16 contributed to record warm years and Great Barrier Reef bleaching.

Gilbert Walker first identified the Southern Oscillation atmospheric pattern in 1924 working with Indian Meteorological Department records. Jacob Bjerknes (1969) linked the atmospheric and oceanic components.
items.why: Global weather has oscillatory components. Forecasts months ahead are skilful when the ENSO state is known — and crops, water supplies and disaster planning across multiple continents depend on the call.

items.title: Most rainforest soils are highly weathered and nutrient-poor
items.claim: What surprises about tropical rainforest soil?

options.text: They are deep and extremely fertile

Heavy rainfall leaches soluble nutrients, leaving iron- and aluminium-rich oxisols (latosols); fertility is held in the biomass and recycled rapidly through litter — slash-and-burn agriculture works for only 2-3 years before fertility crashes
They are pure sand with no organic matter

items.reveal_title: Fertility in the trees, not the ground
items.reveal:
High rainfall and temperatures leach soluble nutrients (calcium, potassium, phosphorus) out of the upper soil, leaving heavily weathered, iron-rich red soils. Decomposition is rapid; mycorrhizal networks and shallow root mats intercept nutrients immediately.

Amazonian 'terra preta' (black earth) soils are a notable exception — anthropogenic soils created by pre-Columbian populations using charcoal, bone and food waste, retaining fertility for centuries. They are now studied as a biochar model.

When forest is cleared, the burn temporarily releases biomass nutrients; crops grow for 2-3 years before yields collapse.
items.why: Lush vegetation does not imply fertile soil. The 'rainforest = rich land' assumption has driven destructive agricultural expansion for centuries — and explains why cleared land degrades quickly.

items.title: Gentrification raises rents and displaces residents
items.claim: What is the core mechanism of gentrification?

options.text: Wealthy newcomers move into deprived neighbourhoods, raising rents and property prices, often displacing existing residents who can no longer afford to stay
Demolition of inner-city housing by the state alone
A spontaneous improvement in services without displacement
An exclusively positive process with no losers

items.reveal:
Ruth Glass coined the term in 1964 in 'London: Aspects of Change', describing changes in Islington. Neil Smith's 'rent gap' theory (1979) explains gentrification by the gap between actual and potential rent in disinvested areas.

London examples: Notting Hill (1960s onwards), Brixton (2000s onwards), Hackney (2000s). New York: SoHo, Williamsburg. Berlin: Prenzlauer Berg, Kreuzberg.

London now has displacement-mitigation policies (affordable housing quotas, right-to-return clauses on estate redevelopment), though their effectiveness is debated.
items.why: Urban regeneration creates both winners and losers. Glossy 'rejuvenation' narratives obscure the costs to displaced residents — and the question of who the city is being improved for.
